questions.question:
D7 — Structure: with RequestPolicy deferred and TokenStore folded, which class arrangement do we build?
Project/branch/task: gstack-plan-count-FkY8wp on main, PLAN.md Multi-tenant Auth Refactor.
ELI10: Three arrangements deliver the same features (D4-D6 held fixed, legacy flow untouched behind a flag). A) three classes: AuthBroker and SessionMint as services, AuthCache as the one facade over the existing adapter. B) two classes: drop the AuthCache facade and let both services call the existing adapter directly, since it already keys by tenant/issuer/audience/policy version. C) one service: merge AuthBroker and SessionMint into a single AuthService over the adapter. The facade matters because two services write to one cache; a single seam is where you put the write discipline and the test double.
Stakes if we pick wrong: too many layers and you maintain a pass-through class; too few and cache write rules get duplicated in two services or one service grows into a god object.
Recommendation: A because both services mutate the same cache (PLAN.md:19-20); one facade is the only place to enforce a single write path and to mock in tests, and it costs one small class. (human: A ~3 days, B ~2.5 days, C ~2 days / CC: A ~40 min, B ~35 min, C ~30 min)
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Net: one deliberate seam for shared-cache writes vs. fewer files with the write rules spread across callers.

options.label: A) 3 classes: Broker, Mint, AuthCache facade (recommended)
options.description: ✅ Single seam for every cache mutation from both services; the concurrency fix lands once. ✅ AuthCache is the natural test double and the natural home for the strangler flag check. ❌ One more class than strictly necessary; the facade must stay thin or it becomes a second adapter.

options.label: B) 2 classes: services use adapter directly
options.description: ✅ Fewest new files; the adapter already has the right tenant-scoped keys and invalidation hooks. ✅ No pass-through layer to keep honest. ❌ Write discipline (who may mutate, in what order) gets duplicated in AuthBroker and SessionMint, the DRY smell the review will flag next.

options.label: C) 1 merged AuthService
options.description: ✅ Smallest possible surface; one class, one test suite. ✅ No shared-cache coordination between services because there is only one service. ❌ Brokering and session minting are different responsibilities with different failure modes; one class grows into the god object the refactor was meant to avoid.

answers.D7 \u2014 Structure: with RequestPolicy: A) 3 classes: Broker, Mint, AuthCache facade (recommended)

questions.question:
D8 — R1: how does the shared AuthCache reach AuthBroker and SessionMint?
Project/branch/task: gstack-plan-count-FkY8wp on main, PLAN.md Multi-tenant Auth Refactor.
ELI10: Today the plan exports one AuthCache from a module and both services import it (PLAN.md:19-20). That works until you need a second instance (a test, a per-region cache) and discover every import is welded to the same object. Constructor injection means the app's startup code builds one AuthCache and hands it to both services; production still has one instance, tests get a fresh one each.
Stakes if we pick wrong: module export leaves tests order-dependent and hides the coupling the refactor exists to remove; injection adds one composition-root file.
Recommendation: A because it is the Layer 1 fix for shared mutable singletons and costs one constructor parameter per service. (human: ~3h / CC: ~10 min)
Completeness: A=10/10, B=3/10, C=6/10
Net: explicit wiring you can see in one file vs. implicit wiring you discover in a flaky test.

options.label: A) Constructor injection (recommended)
options.description: ✅ One AuthCache built at the composition root and passed to both services; production shape unchanged. ✅ Every test gets an isolated instance; no shared-state flakes. ❌ Adds a composition-root file and a constructor parameter to each service.

options.label: B) Keep module-level export
options.description: ✅ Zero extra wiring; matches the original plan text. ✅ Fewest files touched. ❌ Test isolation requires module-cache resets; coupling stays hidden; cannot compose a second instance.

options.label: C) Service locator / getter
options.description: ✅ Central registry, swappable in tests via a setter. ✅ No constructor changes. ❌ Dependencies still invisible at the call site; the setter is global mutable state by another name.

questions.question:
D9 — R2: who may write to AuthCache, and how do writes respect invalidation?
Project/branch/task: gstack-plan-count-FkY8wp on main, PLAN.md Multi-tenant Auth Refactor.
ELI10: Both services write to one cache with no ordering (PLAN.md:10, :20). Picture a tenant getting suspended while SessionMint is halfway through minting a session: the suspension wipes the tenant's entries, then the mint finishes and writes a brand-new one. The suspended tenant now has a working session. Fix options: make SessionMint the only writer and have each write carry the invalidation version it read (write is rejected if the version moved); or let both write but dedupe in-flight work per key and still version-check; or leave it and rely on token expiry.
Stakes if we pick wrong: a revoked or suspended tenant keeps a live session until TTL; that is a security incident, not a cache bug.
Recommendation: A because one writer plus a version check is the smallest change that closes the race, and AuthBroker has no reason to write (it validates). (human: ~1 day / CC: ~20 min)
Completeness: A=10/10, B=9/10, C=2/10
Net: a simple rule (one writer, versioned writes) vs. coordination logic in two places vs. accepting the race.

options.label: A) Single writer + version check (recommended)
options.description: ✅ Only SessionMint writes; AuthBroker is read-only, so there is exactly one write path to test. ✅ Write carries the invalidation version it observed; a suspension between read and write rejects the stale mint. ❌ AuthBroker must ask SessionMint (or the facade) to persist anything it learns; slightly more ceremony.

options.label: B) Per-key in-flight dedupe + version check, both write
options.description: ✅ Concurrent mints for the same key collapse to one IDP round-trip. ✅ Version check still closes the suspension race. ❌ Two writers to test and reason about; the dedupe map is more shared mutable state to get right.

options.label: C) Keep unserialized
options.description: ✅ No new code; matches the original plan. ✅ Fastest to ship. ❌ Suspension/revocation race stays open; a suspended tenant can hold a session until expiry. Fails the security bar for an auth refactor.

questions.question:
D10 — R3: strangler flag granularity for routing tenants to the new services?
Project/branch/task: gstack-plan-count-FkY8wp on main, PLAN.md Multi-tenant Auth Refactor.
ELI10: D6 keeps legacyAuthFlow() running and routes some traffic to AuthBroker/SessionMint behind a flag. A single on/off flag moves every tenant at once. A per-tenant allowlist lets you move one internal tenant first, watch it, then widen; a global kill switch still exists for emergencies. The cache adapter is already tenant-keyed, so per-tenant costs one lookup.
Stakes if we pick wrong: global-only means your first production test of the new auth path is every customer at the same time; per-tenant adds a small config surface to maintain.
Recommendation: A because auth is the one place a canary is non-negotiable and the tenant key is already in hand. (human: ~2h / CC: ~10 min)
Completeness: A=10/10, B=6/10
Net: staged rollout you can reverse per tenant vs. one switch for everyone.

options.label: A) Per-tenant allowlist + global kill switch (recommended)
options.description: ✅ Canary one tenant, then widen; rollback is per tenant or global. ✅ Reuses the tenant key already threaded through every request. ❌ Small config surface (allowlist source, who edits it) to document and test.

options.label: B) Single global boolean
options.description: ✅ Simplest possible flag; one line to flip. ✅ No allowlist to maintain. ❌ First real traffic on the new path is all tenants at once; a bug is a full outage, not a canary blip.

answers.D10 \u2014 R3: strangler flag granularit: A) Per-tenant allowlist + global kill switch (recommended)

questions.question:
D11 — R4: how should validateAndDispatch() handle errors?
Project/branch/task: gstack-plan-count-FkY8wp on main, PLAN.md Multi-tenant Auth Refactor.
ELI10: PLAN.md:23-24 describes a 60-line function with three nested try/catch blocks where each catch quietly eats one kind of error. In an auth path that means a request can fail for three different reasons and the caller sees the same nothing. The complete fix splits the function into named steps and puts one catch at the boundary that turns each failure into a typed error (TokenInvalid, IdpUnavailable, CacheUnavailable) and rethrows it, so the HTTP layer can pick 401 vs 503 and logs say what happened.
Stakes if we pick wrong: keep swallowing and on-call cannot tell an IDP outage from a bad token at 3am; users get a generic failure with no retry hint.
Recommendation: A because AuthBroker will call this function and its errors feed R6's fail-fast; swallowed errors would defeat both. (human: ~1 day / CC: ~15 min)
Completeness: A=10/10, B=5/10, C=1/10
Net: explicit typed failures vs. quiet fallthrough you debug in production.

options.label: A) Flatten + typed AuthError, rethrow (recommended)
options.description: ✅ Each former swallowed class becomes a typed error the HTTP layer maps to 401/403/503 with a clear message. ✅ Function shrinks to sequential named steps; one test per error class. ❌ Callers that relied on silent undefined must now handle a throw; find them via grep.

options.label: B) Keep nesting, log inside each catch
options.description: ✅ Smallest diff; errors at least appear in logs. ✅ No caller changes. ❌ Callers still get silent fallthrough; 60 lines and three nesting levels remain; logs without propagation do not help the user.

options.label: C) Leave as is
options.description: ✅ No work now. ✅ Zero regression risk in this function. ❌ The new AuthBroker inherits a dispatcher that hides IDP outages and bad tokens alike.

questions.question:
D12 — R5 (Iron Rule): what regression contract protects legacyAuthFlow() and proves the new path is equivalent?
Project/branch/task: gstack-plan-count-FkY8wp on main, PLAN.md Multi-tenant Auth Refactor.
ELI10: PLAN.md:14-16 plans zero tests around legacyAuthFlow(). With D6, legacy stays untouched, but two things are still at risk: tenants with the flag off must still reach legacy exactly as before, and tenants with the flag on must get an equivalent session. Behavior to preserve: legacy outputs for success, expired token, revoked token, wrong audience, suspended tenant. Intentional changes: none on the legacy path. Acceptance: a characterization suite pins those five legacy outcomes; a parity test runs the same fixtures through both paths and asserts equivalent session claims and equivalent error class.
Stakes if we pick wrong: a regression in every tenant's login with no test that would have caught it; you find out from customers.
Recommendation: A because with CC the full suite costs minutes and this is the login path for every tenant. (human: ~1.5 days / CC: ~25 min)
Completeness: A=10/10, B=7/10, C=3/10
Net: pinned legacy behavior plus proven equivalence vs. trusting the flag.

options.label: A) Characterization suite + parity test (recommended)
options.description: ✅ Five legacy outcomes pinned before any routing change; a future legacy deletion has a spec to satisfy. ✅ Parity test proves the new path is a drop-in for the same inputs, including error classes. ❌ Requires fixtures for expired, revoked, wrong-audience, suspended cases; the IDP must be stubbed.

options.label: B) Parity test only
options.description: ✅ Proves equivalence on the fixtures you provide. ✅ Less fixture work. ❌ Legacy behavior itself is never pinned; if both paths drift together the test still passes.

options.label: C) Flag-off smoke test only
options.description: ✅ One test, minutes of work. ✅ Confirms routing to legacy still happens. ❌ Says nothing about what legacy or the new path actually return; regression in either goes unnoticed.

questions.question:
D13 — R6: how should the 5 IDP calls run in parallel?
Project/branch/task: gstack-plan-count-FkY8wp on main, PLAN.md Multi-tenant Auth Refactor.
ELI10: PLAN.md:31-32 says the 5 IDP calls are independent and sequential today, so login waits 5 round-trips when it could wait one. Promise.all runs them together and fails the moment any one fails, which is right for validation: one failed check means the token is not valid, so stop. Add a per-call timeout and an overall deadline with AbortController so a hung IDP does not hold the request open. Promise.allSettled instead waits for all five and reports every failure, useful for diagnostics but always as slow as the slowest call.
Stakes if we pick wrong: no timeout means one slow IDP endpoint pins connections; allSettled means users wait for the slowest call even when the first already failed.
Recommendation: A because validation is all-or-nothing and fail-fast with a deadline is the built-in that fits. (human: ~4h / CC: ~10 min)
Completeness: A=10/10, B=8/10, C=2/10
Net: fastest possible answer with a hard ceiling vs. fuller diagnostics at the cost of latency.

options.label: A) Promise.all + per-call timeout + deadline abort (recommended)
options.description: ✅ Login latency drops from 5x to ~1x IDP round-trip; first failure aborts the rest. ✅ Hard deadline means a hung IDP becomes a typed 503, not a stuck request. ❌ Aborted calls' partial failures are not reported; only the first error surfaces.

options.label: B) Promise.allSettled, aggregate errors
options.description: ✅ Every failing check is reported in one error; best for debugging IDP misconfiguration. ✅ Still ~1x round-trip when all succeed. ❌ Waits for the slowest call even after a definitive failure; still needs the same timeout work.

options.label: C) Keep sequential
options.description: ✅ No change; simplest to reason about. ✅ Natural short-circuit on first failure. ❌ Every login pays 5 round-trips; the plan itself calls the fix trivial.

answers.D13 \u2014 R6: how should the 5 IDP call: A) Promise.all + per-call timeout + deadline abort (recommended)

# Plan: Multi-tenant Auth Refactor

Reviewed target: `PLAN.md` (repo root, branch `main`) — /plan-eng-review, 2026-09-15.

## Context
The auth path is being split into tenant-aware services (`AuthBroker`,
`SessionMint`) over a shared cache facade (`AuthCache`) so that token
validation, session minting and cache invalidation have one owner each
instead of living inside `legacyAuthFlow()` and `validateAndDispatch()`.
This review kept the existing cache adapter contract fixed, cut the
proposal from 5 new components to 3, replaced the in-place rewrite with a
per-tenant strangler, and turned every "known problem" the original plan
described (global mutable cache, swallowed errors, no regression tests,
sequential IDP calls) into an accepted, testable remedy.

## Existing contracts retained (unchanged)
The existing cache adapter keys entries by tenant ID, issuer, audience,
and policy version. It evicts expired tokens and invalidates entries on
logout, token revocation, or tenant suspension. The adapter, its
invalidation hooks, and their existing tests remain in use unchanged.
`AuthCache` is a service-facing facade over that same adapter, with one
backing cache, and retains its validity and tenant-key rules. Correction
to the original text: the adapter still does not serialize mutations, but
`AuthCache` now guards writes with a per-tenant invalidation generation
(R2/D8), so a stale write cannot re-insert a token after invalidation.

## Architecture (accepted)
```
request ──> legacyAuthFlow(ctx)            (signature unchanged, D5)
              │
              ├─ selectAuthPath(tenantId)  (D9)
              │    kill switch on ──────────────> legacy body ──> AuthOutcome
              │    tenant ∈ allowlist ─────┐
              │    else / no tenant ───────┼──────> legacy body ──> AuthOutcome
              │                            ▼
              └────────────────────> AuthBroker.authenticate(ctx)
                                         │
                                         ├─ validate(ctx)  ──> AuthOutcome   (D10)
                                         │    ├─ authCache.get(tenant, iss, aud, policyVer) ─ hit ─> allowed
                                         │    └─ miss ─> validateWithIdp(ctx, signal)         (D12)
                                         │               5 concurrent IDP calls, one AbortController,
                                         │               deadline IDP_VALIDATION_DEADLINE_MS
                                         │               any failure/timeout ─> idpUnavailable, abort rest
                                         └─ dispatch(ctx, outcome)   only when outcome = allowed

SessionMint.mint(ctx) ──> authCache.set(key, session, gen)   (gen from prior get)

Composition root (D7)
  adapter (existing) ──> new AuthCache(adapter) ──┬──> new AuthBroker(authCache, idpClient)
                                                  └──> new SessionMint(authCache)
  No module-level AuthCache export anywhere.

AuthCache write guard (D8)
  invalidate*(tenant): gen[tenant]++ ; adapter.invalidate(...) (existing hook, unchanged)
  set(key, value, gen): gen == gen[key.tenant] ? adapter.set : drop + log{tenant, expectedGen, currentGen, caller}
```

Components: `AuthBroker`, `SessionMint`, `AuthCache` (3 new). `TokenStore`
folded into `AuthCache` (D6). `RequestPolicy` deferred (D4). `AuthCache`
methods take `tenantId` as a required parameter; there is no default tenant.

## Code quality (accepted)
`validateAndDispatch()` is split into `validate(ctx): AuthOutcome` and
`dispatch(ctx, outcome)`. One `AuthOutcome` discriminated union
(`allowed | denied(reason) | expired | tenantSuspended | idpUnavailable`)
is defined once and shared by `legacyAuthFlow()`, `AuthBroker` and
`SessionMint`. Exactly one boundary try/catch maps the three
previously-swallowed error classes to outcomes; every other error is
rethrown. `selectAuthPath()` is defined once and called once at
`legacyAuthFlow()` entry.

## Tests (accepted)
Characterization tests pin `legacyAuthFlow()`'s current outcomes for eight
input classes before any delegation is added. A differential harness runs
the legacy body and the `AuthBroker` path on the same fixtures and asserts
identical `AuthOutcome` except an explicit `INTENDED_DIFFERENCES` map (the
D10 error surfacing). One E2E covers flag off and flag on for an
allowlisted tenant. Unit tests cover every branch in the coverage diagram
below. Existing adapter tests are unchanged.

## Performance (accepted)
`validateWithIdp()` fires the 5 independent IDP calls concurrently under one
`AbortController` with deadline `IDP_VALIDATION_DEADLINE_MS` (set from IDP
p99 at implementation; record the measured value in the PR). Any rejection,
429, or the deadline yields `idpUnavailable` and aborts the remaining calls.
Nothing is cached on a non-`allowed` outcome. Cache hit skips all 5 calls
(assumption to confirm against the current code: cache lookup precedes IDP
validation).

## Rollout
1. Land with allowlist empty and kill switch off: every tenant on legacy.
2. Allowlist one internal tenant; watch `idpUnavailable` rate, stale-write
   log lines, and differential-harness parity in CI.
3. Widen the allowlist in cohorts; kill switch reverts all tenants at once.
4. After 100% allowlist for N quiet days, run the D13 cleanup TODO.

## Architecture (scope smell, original)
Original proposal: 12 files, 5 new components (AuthBroker, SessionMint,
AuthCache, TokenStore, RequestPolicy; the original text said "4" and omitted
AuthBroker).

## Scope decisions (Step 0, accepted)
- **D4 — `RequestPolicy` deferred** to a follow-up PR. It had no stated
  contract, callers, or behavior. Follow-up must specify inputs, tenant rules,
  and failure behavior before it touches auth.
- **D5 — `legacyAuthFlow()` strangled, not rewritten in place.** It keeps
  its signature and callers. Its body delegates to `AuthBroker`/`SessionMint`
  when a feature flag is on; flag off keeps today's body. Legacy body and
  flag are removed in a follow-up PR after the new path has carried traffic.
- **D6 — `TokenStore` folded into `AuthCache`.** One service-facing facade
  owns tenant/issuer/audience/policy-version key construction and
  invalidation calls on top of the existing adapter. No second store.
- Resulting new components: `AuthBroker`, `SessionMint`, `AuthCache` (3).
  File count drops from 12 (estimate: 9-10 after the two removals; recount
  during implementation).

## Decision ledger

### R1: How AuthBroker and SessionMint obtain the AuthCache instance
Finding: A1, P1, confidence 9/10, PLAN.md:19-20 ("share a global mutable
`AuthCache` instance via module-level export. Both services mutate it"),
reviewer: Claude (plan-eng-review)
Plan baseline: module-level exported mutable singleton (original proposal)
Runtime evidence: unknown; no implementation exists yet. Web research
[Layer 1]: exporting a mutable instance is the documented Node singleton
footgun; export a factory/class and inject instead.
State: approved

Comparison grid:

| Choice | Current | A inject | B keep global | C global + readonly getter |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| R1 cache acquisition | module-level mutable export, pending | constructor injection from one composition root; no module-level instance | module-level export (unchanged) | module-level instance behind a getter; mutation only via AuthCache methods |
| Adapter key/invalidation contract (PLAN.md:7-13) | retained, approved | retained | retained | retained |
| R2 mutation serialization | unspecified, pending | pending | pending | pending |
| R3 strangler flag scope | unspecified, pending | pending | pending | pending |

Question D7:
D7 — Should AuthBroker and SessionMint receive AuthCache by injection instead of importing a module-level global?
Options: A) Constructor injection from one composition root (recommended);
B) Keep the module-level mutable export as planned; C) Keep a module-level
instance but expose it only through a getter, mutations only via AuthCache
methods. Completeness: A=10/10, B=3/10, C=6/10.

Actual answer: A — constructor injection (D7 answer)
Accepted scope: one composition root constructs AuthCache (over the existing
adapter) and passes it to AuthBroker and SessionMint constructors. No
module-level AuthCache instance is exported. Tests construct a fresh
AuthCache per case. Necessary proof: unit test that two service instances
built with different AuthCache instances do not observe each other's writes.
History: none

### R2: Protection against write-after-invalidate on the shared cache
Finding: A2, P1, confidence 8/10, PLAN.md:10 ("they do not serialize
mutations") + PLAN.md:20 ("Both services mutate it") + PLAN.md:8-9
(invalidation on logout, revocation, tenant suspension), reviewer: Claude
Plan baseline: no serialization; both services write freely (original
proposal). The adapter's invalidation hooks are retained unchanged (approved,
PLAN.md:12-13).
Runtime evidence: unknown; whether the adapter offers atomic
compare-and-set or generation counters is unverified. Pattern: SessionMint
reads/validates, tenant gets suspended and adapter invalidates, SessionMint's
in-flight write then re-inserts a token for a suspended tenant.
State: approved

Comparison grid:

| Choice | Current | A generation guard | B document, accept | C investigate adapter first |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| R2 write-after-invalidate protection | none, pending | AuthCache is sole writer; per-tenant invalidation generation; a write carrying a stale generation is dropped and logged | none; documented as known race | pending until a bounded probe of the adapter API |
| R1 cache acquisition | constructor injection (D7) | fixed | fixed | fixed |
| Adapter contract (PLAN.md:7-13) | retained, approved | retained (generation lives in AuthCache, adapter untouched) | retained | retained |
| R3 strangler flag scope | pending | pending | pending | pending |

Question D8:
D8 — Should AuthCache guard against a stale in-flight write re-inserting
a token after invalidation? Options: A) Per-tenant invalidation generation
in AuthCache; stale writes dropped and logged (recommended); B) Accept and
document the race; C) Probe the existing adapter for atomic primitives before
choosing. Completeness: A=10/10, B=3/10; C is an investigation, unscored.

Actual answer: A — per-tenant invalidation generation guard (D8 answer)
Accepted scope: AuthCache is the only writer to the adapter. AuthCache keeps
a per-tenant invalidation generation (monotonic integer). Reads return the
generation alongside the value; writes carry the generation they were based
on; AuthCache drops a write whose generation is stale and logs
{tenantId, expectedGen, currentGen, caller}. AuthCache's invalidation entry
points (logout, revocation, suspension) bump the generation, then call the
adapter's existing invalidation hook unchanged. Generation map is bounded:
entries for tenants with no cached keys are pruned on invalidation. Necessary
proof: unit tests for stale-write-dropped, fresh-write-accepted,
generation-bumps-per-invalidation, and prune behavior; one integration test
for the suspend-during-mint race.
History: none

### R3: Scope of the strangler flag for legacyAuthFlow()
Finding: A3, P2, confidence 7/10, follows from D5 (strangler accepted) —
the plan text (PLAN.md:27-28) has no flag; D5 introduced one without
choosing its granularity. Reviewer: Claude
Plan baseline: flag exists (D5); granularity unspecified, pending
Runtime evidence: unknown; no flag infrastructure has been inspected.
State: approved

Comparison grid:

| Choice | Current | A per-tenant allowlist + global kill switch | B global boolean |
|---|---|---|---|
| R3 flag scope | unspecified, pending | route to new path if tenantId in allowlist AND kill switch off; else legacy | one process-wide boolean |
| R1 cache acquisition | injection (D7) | fixed | fixed |
| R2 generation guard | approved (D8) | fixed | fixed |
| D5 strangler (signature retained, delegating body) | approved | fixed | fixed |

Question D9:
D9 — How granular should the legacyAuthFlow() cutover flag be? Options:
A) Per-tenant allowlist plus a global kill switch (recommended); B) Single
global boolean. Completeness: A=10/10, B=7/10.

Actual answer: A — per-tenant allowlist + global kill switch (D9 answer)
Accepted scope: one routing function `selectAuthPath(tenantId)` returns
`legacy` or `broker`. Rule: kill switch on → legacy; else tenantId in
allowlist → broker; else legacy. Missing/empty tenantId → legacy (never the
new path). legacyAuthFlow() calls this once at entry. Necessary proof: unit
tests for all four rule branches plus the missing-tenant case; kill switch
precedence over allowlist asserted explicitly.
History: none

### R4: Error handling shape of validateAndDispatch()
Finding: C1, P1, confidence 9/10, PLAN.md:23-24 ("60 lines with three
nested try/catch blocks; each catch swallows a different error class"),
reviewer: Claude
Plan baseline: three nested try/catch, each swallowing one error class
(original proposal; the plan describes it but proposes no change)
Runtime evidence: unknown; described in the plan, code not inspected.
State: approved

Comparison grid:

| Choice | Current | A split + explicit error map | B keep nesting, log in each catch | C leave as-is |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| R4 error handling | 3 nested catches, swallow, pending | `validate()` and `dispatch()` separated; one boundary catch maps known error classes to explicit typed outcomes (e.g. `AuthOutcome.denied(reason)`); unknown errors rethrown; nothing swallowed | same structure, each catch logs then swallows | unchanged |
| R1/R2/R3/D4-D6 | approved | fixed | fixed | fixed |

Question D10:
D10 — Refactor validateAndDispatch() so no error is swallowed? Options:
A) Split validate/dispatch; single boundary catch mapping known error
classes to typed outcomes, unknown rethrown (recommended); B) Keep the
three nested catches but log in each; C) Leave as-is.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=5/10, C=1/10.

Actual answer: A — split + explicit error map (D10 answer)
Accepted scope: `validateAndDispatch()` becomes `validate(ctx): AuthOutcome`
and `dispatch(ctx, outcome)`. One `AuthOutcome` discriminated union
(e.g. `allowed`, `denied(reason)`, `expired`, `tenantSuspended`,
`idpUnavailable`) defined once and shared by legacyAuthFlow(), AuthBroker
and SessionMint. Exactly one try/catch at the boundary maps the three
previously-swallowed error classes to outcomes; any other error is
rethrown. Necessary proof: one unit test per mapped error class → outcome,
one for unknown-error-rethrown, one asserting dispatch never runs on a
non-`allowed` outcome.
History: none

### R5: Regression coverage for legacyAuthFlow() current behavior
Finding: T1, P1 (CRITICAL), confidence 9/10, PLAN.md:27-28 ("will get
rewritten ... no regression test for the prior behavior is planned") and
PLAN.md:14-16 ("does not exercise legacyAuthFlow() or assert compatibility
with its prior behavior"), reviewer: Claude. IRON RULE: a rewrite (or
strangler delegation) is a regression risk; coverage is required, the
question is how.
Plan baseline: no regression coverage (original proposal)
Runtime evidence: unknown; legacyAuthFlow() callers and behavior not
inspected (no implementation in this fixture repo).
State: approved

Comparison grid:

D8 — Should AuthCache guard against a stale in-flight write re-inserting a token after invalidation?
Project/branch/task: main, PLAN.md "Multi-tenant Auth Refactor"; Architecture finding A2 (P1, 8/10), PLAN.md:10 + :20 + :8-9.
ELI10: The plan says two services write to the cache and nothing serializes those writes (PLAN.md:10, :20). Meanwhile the adapter wipes a tenant's entries on logout, revocation or suspension (PLAN.md:8-9). questions.question:
D12 — How should the 5 IDP validation calls be parallelized?
Project/branch/task: main, PLAN.md "Multi-tenant Auth Refactor"; Performance finding (P2, 8/10), PLAN.md:31-32.
ELI10: Today validation makes 5 round trips to the identity provider one after another, so a user waits 5× the IDP latency. The plan says "just use Promise.all", which fires all 5 at once and waits for all. Correct, but bare Promise.all has two sharp edges: if one call fails, the other four keep running and burning IDP quota, and if the IDP is slow there is no deadline, so the request hangs as long as the slowest call. Wrapping the five in one AbortSignal with a deadline fixes both: any failure or timeout cancels the rest and becomes a typed `idpUnavailable` outcome the user can understand.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Bare Promise.all turns an IDP brownout into requests that hang until the socket gives up, with four orphaned calls each; sequential keeps users waiting 5× longer than needed forever.
Recommendation: A because it is Promise.all plus about ten lines (signal, deadline, mapping to the D10 outcome) and turns "IDP slow" from a hang into a fast, clear failure (human: ~3h incl. tests / CC: ~10 min).
Completeness: A=10/10, B=7/10, C=3/10
Net: bounded, cancellable fan-out vs. the bare one-liner vs. status quo latency.

options.label: Promise.all under one AbortSignal with a deadline; failure or timeout → idpUnavailable, rest aborted (recommended)
options.description:
✅ Latency drops from ~5× to ~1× IDP round trip and is capped by an explicit deadline, so a slow IDP produces a fast, typed failure.
✅ First failure aborts the other four calls; no orphaned requests eating IDP rate limit during an outage.
❌ One tunable (the deadline) to pick from IDP p99 and keep honest; one AbortSignal to thread into the HTTP client.

options.label: Bare Promise.all as proposed
options.description:
✅ Literally one line; gets the 5× latency win immediately.
✅ No new config value.
❌ No deadline: a slow IDP hangs the request; a failed call leaves four still running; rejection surfaces as a raw error, not an AuthOutcome.

options.label: Keep the 5 sequential calls
options.description:
✅ Zero change to the validation path in an already large refactor.
✅ Naturally gentle on IDP rate limits.
❌ Every authenticated request pays 5 round trips when 1 would do; the plan itself calls this trivially fixable.
